中文.来源: 大模型翻译（基于日文条目）

英文.首段: The 32 series electric multiple unit (32-kei densha) is a collective name applied for convenience to the two-door, cross-seat old-type (prewar) electric multiple units that the Ministry of Railways — the predecessor of Japanese National Railways (JNR) — introduced for the Yokosuka Line between 1930 and 1932.

章节.Background of introduction:
The Yokosuka Line was built at the request of both the Imperial Japanese Army and Navy to transport to Yokosuka — a naval port city housing a naval district headquarters — to the Kannonzaki Battery, one of the coastal batteries of the Army's Tokyo Bay Fortress, and to Nagai, one of the points where an enemy landing was anticipated. Because it was regarded as a militarily important line, work such as double-tracking was carried out from an early date, and by December 25, 1924, double-tracking as far as Yokosuka, then the terminus, had been completed. In 1922, electrification work was begun together with the Tokyo–Odawara section of the Tokaido Main Line; although it was temporarily suspended by the Great Kanto Earthquake the following year, work resumed in April 1924 and was completed in July 1925. From December 13 of that year, locomotive-hauled passenger trains began operating.

However, the population along the line increased year by year thereafter and traffic volume grew; with the resulting increase in the number of trains, the introduction of electric multiple units came to be considered advantageous, and because there was also a need to counter the Shonan Electric Railway, which opened in 1930, a plan was drawn up to replace the Yokosuka Line's trains with electric multiple units. The units introduced under this plan were the 32 series described in this article. Electric operation on the Yokosuka Line began on March 15, 1930, but because the 32 series cars were not ready in time, initially a total of 101 cars were used, assembled from the Chuo and Keihin lines: 33 MoHa 30, 18 MoHa 31, 16 KuHa 15, 14 SaHa 25, 3 SaHa 36, and 17 SaRo 18. The basic formation was six cars and the supplementary (attached) formation was three cars.

Thereafter, a total of 111 cars of the 32 series were allocated to the Tamachi Electric Car Depot (which became Tamachi Electric Car District in 1936) from February 1931 and entered service on April 1. About a year later, in July 1932, they replaced the existing electric cars, and under the timetable revised on October 1, 1931, 44 round trips were operated between Tokyo and Yokosuka in 58 minutes. As for the combined mail, baggage, and third-class cars, four MoHaYuni 30 cars of the 30 series continued to be used alongside the 32 series after its introduction; in 1935, five MoHaYuni 44 cars of the 42 series were introduced to replace them, and in 1943 four more MoHaYuni 61 cars of the 51 series were added. Also, until the KuRo 49 cars built under the 1931 fiscal year budget were introduced, the imperial-family passenger car NaiRoFu 20550 was coupled to the electric cars in service.
章节.Overview:
=== Body ===
In planning this series, because the cars would run the 62.4 km between Tokyo and Yokosuka — a long distance unprecedented for a Ministry of Railways line at the time — it was decided, in order to secure as many seating positions as possible, to give the third-class cars two doors per side as well, following the Type 43200 cars built from 1922 in connection with the electrification of the Tokyo–Odawara section. The passenger doors were placed as close to the car ends as possible, with box seats arranged between them. However, to ease congestion near the doors and to install door engines, the cars did not adopt a structure with end platforms at both ends of the body as in passenger cars; instead the passenger doors were set within the passenger compartment, with windows and longitudinal benches between the doors and the car ends. The cars were also the first electric cars within the jurisdiction of the Tokyo Railway Bureau to be fitted with gangway bellows and sliding doors at the car ends, and they formed formations basically made up solely of cars of the same series — marking a clear departure from conventional Ministry of Railways electric cars.

Another feature of the series was that, in order to lengthen the body and secure seating capacity, it adopted 20 m-class car bodies for the trailer and control cars — the first such use for a Ministry of Railways electric car. The 20 m-class body had been used for wooden passenger cars since the Railway Institute standard-type passenger cars introduced from 1910 onward, and this series used the UF23 underframe, following the UF22 underframe structure with a channel-steel centre sill used in the SuHa 32 series.

The motor cars, on the other hand, retained the conventional 17 m-class body. This was because the traction motors remained the MT15 series motors of 100 kW that were the standard of the day, and the length was kept at 17 m in consideration of tractive effort. As for the underframe, as with the MoHa 31 of the 31 series, the cars built in fiscal 1930 (32001–32032) used the fish-belly UF20 underframe with a centre sill assembled from steel plate and angle steel, while from the fiscal 1931 cars (32023–32045) the design shifted to the UF24, which used a channel-steel centre sill.

The body's exterior resembled that of the 31 series, and the vertical dimensions of the side windows and their height above the floor were the same as that series, at 870 mm and 800 mm respectively. As with the 31 series, rain gutters were not fitted owing to clearance-limit constraints, as on the cars built in the early period, but they were fitted from the additional cars onward in response to the enlargement of the vehicle gauge following the enactment of the Government Railways Construction Regulations in August 1929, and cars built earlier were also retrofitted later. The junction between the roof and body at the front was likewise straight as on the 31 series; the headlight was mounted on the cornice, and a whistle was installed above the cab window beside it. From the time of construction, only a single red tail light was provided, and the class band below the side windows was marked only on second-class cars. At the gangway ends, the arrangement changed from the inward-opening gangway door with no bellows used up to the 31 series to a single-sliding gangway door with bellows; second-class cars had no end windows, while third-class cars did.

The side windows were of the two-stage drop type. As for the window arrangement, on third-class cars two 600 mm-wide windows were placed in each box-seat section between the passenger doors, while the door pocket window on the body-centre side of the passenger doors and the window on the gangway side consisted of one 600 mm-wide window each. On second-class cars, by contrast, the box-seat sections between the passenger doors had two 700 mm-wide windows per box as a set, and the windows on the body-centre side of the passenger doors and on the gangway side likewise consisted of a set of two 700 mm-wide windows, of which the one on the body-centre side of the passenger doors was a door pocket window.

=== Interior ===
In the third-class car interior, the gangway-side car end and the section of one window on the body-centre side of the passenger doors had longitudinal benches, while the rest had box seats. The longitudinal benches had a depth of 480 mm including the backrest; the box-seat pitch was 1,400 mm — wider than the 1,300 mm of the Type 43200 and OHa 31, and slightly narrower than the 1,455 mm of the SuHa 32 — with a depth of 450 mm including the backrest, cloth-upholstered cushion seats, and board backrests.

In the second-class car interior, the gangway-side car end and the sections of two windows on the body-centre side of the passenger doors had longitudinal benches, while the rest had cross seats. The longitudinal benches had a depth of 610 mm including the backrest; the box-seat pitch was 1,760 mm — slightly wider than the 1,700 mm of the Type 43200 and narrower than the 1,980 mm of the SuHa 32, and the same as the 31 series — with a depth of 600 mm including the backrest, and the width of the box seats was slightly increased from the 965 mm of the 31 series to 980 mm. In addition, the seats in the second-class compartments were cloth-upholstered cushions on both backrest and seat surface.

In addition, on both second- and third-class cars the passenger doors were 1,100 mm-wide single doors; spittoons (tan-tsubo) were provided on the floor in accordance with the tuberculosis prevention regulations, and straps were fitted to the ceiling above the longitudinal benches. Furthermore, the toilets and washrooms that had been provided on the SaHa 43500 of the Type 43200 were not fitted on the 32 series at the time of construction, except on the KuRo 49 VIP cars.

The arrangement of equipment in the cab was as follows.
Driver's desk: master controller (main controller), brake valve (ME23), duplex pressure gauge, speedometer, control pressure gauge (MoHa 32 only), driver's indicator light, buzzer, buzzer push button
Cab front: at the top, lighting switch, pantograph switch, control switch, 7-point switch board (SH28), 6-point switch board (SH26), relay terminal block, canopy switch for the motor-driven air compressor (MoHa 32 only), canopy switch for the motor-generator (MoHa 32 only), and conductor's valve; at the bottom, dry-battery box, pantograph raise solenoid valve / lower solenoid valve / hand pump (MoHa 32 only), low-voltage auxiliary circuit fuse (MoHa 32 only), and hand brake
Cab side: conductor's switch, buzzer push button
Cab rear: at the top, heating fuse, two heating canopy switches, lighting contactor (two on MoHa 32, one on KuHa 47); at the bottom, door-close changeover switch and air supply valve

=== Main equipment ===
The main controller of the MoHa 32 was the same electromagnetic air camshaft type with five series and four parallel notches as on the 31 series, but from this type onward a CS9 field-weakening contactor made by Shibaura Engineering Works or Hitachi was newly added to provide one parallel field-weakening notch. (The main controllers of Ministry of Railways cars built from fiscal 1927 onward were the CS1 made by Shibaura (maker's type RPC-101) or the CS3 made by Hitachi (maker's type PR200), and from fiscal 1932 onward the CS5, a joint Shibaura–Hitachi design, was fitted.) The master controller was the MC1A. As traction motors, it carried four MT15A motors, derived from the MT15 series jointly designed by the Ministry of Railways and the various manufacturers (Shibaura, Hitachi, Toyo Electric Manufacturing, and Mitsubishi Electric) — with a one-hour rated output of 100 kW at a terminal voltage of 675 V and a rated speed of 653 rpm — but with the field-weakening ratio newly set to 70% in preparation for high-speed operation. The gear ratio was changed from the 31 series' 2.52 to 2.26 in preparation for high-speed running, giving a rated speed of 56 km/h and a tractive effort of 26.5 kN at 70% field weakening (the 31 series gave 42.5 km/h and 33.8 kN at full field). The gears and gear cases were of soundproof specification.

In addition, the pantograph was the PS2 fitted to cars built between fiscal 1916 and fiscal 1931; the motor-generator was the 100 V/2 kW output MH49-DM28 newly adopted from this type; and the motor-driven air compressor was the MH16B-AK3 — one of each being carried on each MoHa 32.

The braking system was the AE electromagnetic air brake used on JNR electric cars up to the 80 series, combining an A control valve with solenoid exhaust valves to accelerate the service and emergency braking actions. Under the floor it carried the A control valve and solenoid exhaust valves together with 356×250 V brake cylinders (MoHa 32) or 305×250 V brake cylinders (cars other than MoHa 32), and an ME23 brake valve was installed in the cab. Cars with a cab were also fitted with a hand brake.

The couplers were automatic couplers at the time of construction, but from the outset provision was made for the eventual adoption of tight-lock couplers in order to eliminate coupler slack. As for the electrical couplers, on the low-voltage jumper side one control connection and one automatic-door/brake connection were provided on the mountain side of the automatic coupler (the right side when viewed facing the down direction), with one control connection on the sea side (the left side); on the high-voltage jumper side a single-core connector was provided on the sea side of the automatic coupler. The 7-core KE50 was used for the low-voltage jumpers and the single-core KE1 for the high-voltage jumper. On both the down (even-numbered) and up (odd-numbered) facing cars, the underfloor equipment layout remained identical while the car was turned, with only the position of the electrical couplers swapped between sea and mountain sides.

=== Bogies ===
The MoHa 32 used the TR22 (later DT11) bogie. This was an equalizer bogie with forged equalizing beams and swing-hanger links suspended from the side frames, with a wheelbase of 2,450 mm and a wheel diameter of 910 mm. It was adopted from the 1928 additional cars of the 30 series electric cars, and the changes from the previous TR14 (later DT10) were as follows.
The equalizing beams were changed from one per side to two.
The bogie frame was changed to an assembled unit with the side frames altered from bulb-angle steel to flat bar steel and the end beams from rolled steel to cast steel.
The upper bolster and swing bolster were changed from assembled rolled steel to cast steel.
Tapered end supports were used at the junction of the upper and lower bolster springs so that the bolster-spring rate varied with load.
The axles were changed from 10 t motor axles to 12 t motor axles, and the wheel diameter from 914 mm to 910 mm.

The KuHa 47, SaHa 48, SaRo 45, and SaRoHa 46 used the TR23. This bogie was a trailer bogie called the Pennsylvania type, adopted from the SuHa 32 series built from 1929 onward. The axlebox support was of the pedestal type, with coil springs placed above the axleboxes; the bolster-spring section had a short-link swing-hanger suspended from the centre of the side frame and connected to the lower swing bolster, with leaf springs arranged as bolster springs between the upper and lower swing bolsters. The bogie frame consisted of side frames in which the integral cast-steel axle-spring caps and the upper parts of the axlebox guides were connected fore and aft by I-beams and the lower parts by flat steel, assembled with cast-steel transoms and end beams; the upper swing bolster was cast steel, the wheelbase was 2,450 mm using 12 t long axles, and the wheel diameter was 860 mm.
章节.Basic types:
=== MoHa 32 ===
This was the control motor car forming the backbone of the series; 32 cars (32001–32032) were built under the fiscal 1930 budget and 13 (32033–32045) under the fiscal 1931 budget. Owing to the formation arrangement, cars 32001–32013 all faced up (odd), and thereafter odd-numbered cars faced up and even-numbered cars faced down. Unlike the other trailer types, this type had a 17 m-class body with a window/door arrangement of dD1121D1 and a capacity of 100 (66 seated); the box seats between the doors numbered six sets per side, and to secure their space the leading passenger door was shifted forward, making the cab-rear portion of the passenger compartment 200 mm narrower than on the KuHa 47, so the body layout was fore-and-aft asymmetrical.

=== SaRo 45 ===
A two-door, box-seat second-class trailer for the basic formation; 10 cars (45001–45010) were built under the fiscal 1930 budget and three (45011–45013) under the fiscal 1931 budget. Initially for the basic formation, they were moved to the supplementary formation around 1935. The window arrangement was 2D2222222D2 with a capacity of 72, resembling a 20 m-class stretching of the SaRo 37 of the 31 series.

=== SaRoHa 46 ===
A combined second- and third-class car for the supplementary formation; 10 cars (46001–46010) were built under the fiscal 1930 budget and three (46011–46013) under the fiscal 1931 budget. Initially for the supplementary formation, they were moved to the basic formation around 1935. The design resembled the SaRo 45 and SaHa 48 joined together. The window arrangement was 2D222261D1 with a capacity of 96 (40 second-class and 36 third-class seats).

=== KuHa 47 ===
A third-class control car for the supplementary formation; 10 cars (47001–47010) were built under the fiscal 1930 budget. Owing to the formation arrangement, all faced down (even). Because of the 20 m-class body, the box seats between the doors numbered eight sets per side, more than on the MoHa 32. The window arrangement was dD1161D1 with a capacity of 120 (82 seated).

=== SaHa 48 ===
An all-third-class trailer; 18 cars (48001–48018) were built under the fiscal 1930 budget and 10 (48019–48028) under the fiscal 1931 budget. The window arrangement was 1D1161D1 with a capacity of 134 (88 seated).

=== KuRo 49 ===
A second-class control car (VIP car), two of which (49001, 49002) were built under the fiscal 1931 budget for the use of the Imperial family; both faced down (even). This type was planned as a replacement for the Type 20550 NaiRoFu 20550 of the 22000-series wooden passenger cars then in use. It was specially ordered because the Yokosuka Line had a demand for VIP cars, such as for members of the Imperial family travelling to and from the Hayama Imperial Villa for summer retreats and for Imperial family members on military service commuting to and from Yokosuka naval port. Unlike a “special imperial train,” it was used coupled to regular trains; although a control car, in actual operation it was basically formed as “(Yokosuka ←) regular train + KuRo 49 + MoHa 32 (→ Tokyo),” so the KuRo 49's cab was almost never at the head of the formation.

In June 1947 (Showa 22), during Emperor Showa's visit to Wakayama Prefecture (the Emperor's postwar tour), KuRo 49001 and 49002 were transferred dead to the Kansai region, with 49002 used for the imperial train and 49001 as a spare. On that occasion, the control circuits and the crest-mounting fittings were modified at the Suita Works.

The window arrangement was d122D2222D2, and the interior layout differed greatly from ordinary cars: immediately behind the cab were a toilet and washroom attached to the special compartment, followed by a 3,900 mm-long special compartment (capacity 10); the side panel at this section was provided with a pedestal for mounting the Imperial crest, and from the passenger door on the cab side rearward was a rest room for attendants (second class, capacity 40). The special compartment had no passenger door; the leading passenger door was placed in the attendants' rest room (second class) immediately behind the special compartment, and because this door was not opened or closed at intermediate stations, it was a manually operated door with no door engine.

The special compartment was 1,750 mm wide (only the leading end-wall section was 926 mm); two sets of box seats with armrests at the ends were placed toward the sea side, with a seat pitch of 1,950 mm and a seat depth of 625 mm. The side windows were, as in the second-class compartments, arranged as sets of two 700 mm-wide windows, and the compartment was provided with a folding table and an electric fan. The toilet was on the mountain side and the washroom on the sea side; the toilet contained a towel rack, luggage rack, and hat hooks, while the washroom contained a mirror, cosmetics shelf, cup stand, liquid-soap holder, mouthwash water tank, towel rack, luggage rack, and hat hooks.

The interior of the attendants' rest room (second class) was basically of the same specification as the second-class compartments of the SaRo 45 and others, except that no longitudinal bench was provided on the body-centre side of the rear passenger door — box seats extended right up beside the door.

章节.Prewar modifications:
=== Modification of front-end equipment ===
The whistle was replaced with an air horn (tyfon) around 1937.

The Shibata-type tight-lock coupler, developed between 1929 and 1931, was field-tested on the Yokosuka Line, and from January 18 to June 4, 1935, the automatic couplers were replaced with tight-lock couplers. Meanwhile, from 1930 a 27-core electrical coupler was installed below the Shibata-type tight-lock coupler on the Yokosuka Line for field tests, but this was not put into practical use for budgetary reasons. The electrical couplers were rearranged so that three low-voltage jumper KE50s were placed on the mountain side of the tight-lock coupler and one high-voltage jumper KE1 on the sea side.

The headlight was relocated onto the roof from 1936 onward.

=== Installation of toilets ===
Because the Yokosuka Line ran long distances, demand grew for toilets, and in 1935 the first installation of toilets on electric cars was carried out on the SaRoHa 46 and SaHa 48 at the Oi Works. The toilets had a water tank under the floor and were the first to use a system of raising water by compressed-air pressure; moreover, as equipment for electric-car toilets, where short turnaround times leave no time for cleaning, they adopted a system that automatically flushed the bowl in conjunction with the opening and closing of the toilet sliding door, and were fitted with a water cock used to clean the toilet floor.

On the SaRoHa 46, the toilet was installed on the third-class side of the partitioned body centre, and the capacity became 91 (40 second-class and 32 third-class seats). At the same time, to distinguish them from the Keihanshin-area SaRoHa 46 cars that had no toilet, the type designation was changed to SaRoHa 66 (66001–66013).

On the SaHa 48, a toilet was installed at the rear end, and the longitudinal bench facing the toilet was converted to box seats, giving a capacity of 124 (86 seated).

=== Conversion of SaRo 45 to SaRoHa 66 ===
Because the SaRo 45 cars originally in the basic formation were moved to the supplementary formation and the SaRoHa 66 cars moved from the supplementary to the basic formation, and in view of the formation arrangement, in 1936 two SaRo 45 cars were converted at the Oi Works by creating a half-compartment third-class area and installing a toilet, becoming SaRoHa 66. There was no major change in appearance — only the two side windows at the toilet section became 600 mm wide — but inside, the third-class compartment differed from other SaRoHa 66 cars, which had three sets of cross seats, in having only two sets, with part of the seat pitch at 1,545 mm, making it irregular; correspondingly the longitudinal bench beside the door was 900 mm longer, at 2,200 mm. The capacity was 99 (40 second-class and 30 third-class seats). The old and new numbers correspond as follows.
66014 ← 45001
66015 ← 45002
As replacements for the two SaRo 45 cars thus removed, SaRo 37 cars 37001 and 37002 of the 31 series, which had been used on the Keihin Line, were transferred. These two cars were notable for having TR21 bogies, and in the transfer they were modified by converting the gangway doors to sliding doors and fitting gangway bellows.

=== Addition of ventilators ===
The roof ventilators of the 32 series originally consisted of a single row of Garland-type ventilators; to improve interior ventilation, in conjunction with the special repair work carried out from fiscal 1937, they were increased to three rows. After about 50 cars had been modified, the work was halted when the wartime system was established in 1938, but the work of opening ventilation holes in the ceiling continued thereafter, so that the cars fell into three forms: three rows of ventilators and three rows of ceiling vents; one row of ventilators and three rows of ceiling vents; and one row of ventilators and one row of ceiling vents.

=== Running gear ===
The MT15A was later modified to the MT15C, with the armature shaft diameter increased from 150 mm to 155 mm.

=== Olympic test livery ===
Ahead of the Tokyo Olympics, which were to have been held in 1940 to commemorate the 2,600th anniversary of the legendary accession of Emperor Jimmu, a change of livery for Ministry of Railways electric cars was planned. In 1938, on the Yokosuka Line, two four-car formations of the 32 series — 32024–48009–66009–32022 and 32036–48010–66010–32025 — received a test livery known as Plan B, with maroon side panels and cream window surrounds, but it was reverted the following year.

=== Side destination blinds ===
Before the war, on steel-bodied electric cars of the Ministry of Railways era, destination blinds were fitted as standard to the side cornice from the 33 and 40 series onward, which were built or re-bodied from 1932. However, SaHa 45004 (formerly SaRo 45004) bears traces of a blocked-off destination blind; whether it dates from construction or from a later modification is unclear, but it was the only such car among the 30, 31, and 32 series, suggesting that it had an experimental aspect.
章节.Wartime modifications:
Even after the wartime system was established, the second-class cars on the Yokosuka Line, which had been retained because of the naval port at Yokosuka, were also to be abolished on April 1, 1944, and a plan was drawn up to add doors and convert the Yokosuka Line cars to longitudinal seating. The plan was to add one passenger door at the body centre of the MoHa 32 to make it a three-door car while keeping the gear ratio unchanged, and to add two doors to the SaRo 45, KuHa 47, SaHa 48, and SaRoHa 66 to make them four-door cars. However, with the worsening course of the Pacific War and the resumption of second-class cars on the Yokosuka Line, only the SaRoHa 66 was modified in full; the SaRo 45 and KuHa 47 were modified only in part, and the MoHa 32 and SaHa 48 were not modified at all, so the plan was abandoned.

Even the cars left unmodified had their interior metal parts, such as handrails, removed and salvaged in 1943; on the Yokosuka Line, from 1944 onward, seat-removal work as a congestion measure was carried out, converting cars to longitudinal benches or to a mix of cross and longitudinal seating, and even after the war modifications continued, including the thinning-out of cross seats. From around May 1948, as part of the work to restore the removed seats, the MoHa 32 cars were progressively converted to all-longitudinal seating.

Meanwhile, as air raids intensified, the five SaRo 45 cars that remained as second-class cars were fitted, toward the Yokosuka end, with a “special compartment” whose surroundings were clad in steel plate for protection against shrapnel.

=== Conversion of SaRoHa 66 to commuter type (SaHa 78) ===
With the abolition of second class, the SaRoHa 66 cars became substitutes for third class, and during fiscal 1944 all were converted to commuter type at the Oi Works and reclassified as SaHa 78, numbered 78009–78023 following the newly built cars of that type. On this occasion the toilets were removed; the window arrangement of 78009–78021 (ex-SaRoHa 46) took the form 2D21D121D21D1, while 78022 and 78023 (ex-SaRo 45) took the same form as the six SaRo 45 cars converted to commuter type described below, namely 2D21D22D12D2, and on none of the cars was a window header fitted above the added doors. The old and new numbers correspond as follows.

=== Conversion of SaRo 45 to commuter type (SaHa 78) ===
With the abolition of second class, this type became a substitute for third class, and it was planned to convert all ten cars other than 45005 — which was to remain a second-class car for the time being as a spare for the VIP cars — to commuter type during fiscal 1944, making them SaHa 78 (78024–78034 ← 45003–45013), following the cars converted from the SaRoHa 66.

However, on August 16 of that year the coupling of second-class cars on the Yokosuka Line was restored, and the plan was changed at the point when six cars had been converted to commuter type at the Oi Works, so five cars — 45004, 45005, 45007, 45008, and 45012 — were retained as second class. The old and new numbers correspond as follows, with gaps arising from the discontinuation of the work.

=== Conversion of KuHa 47 to commuter type (KuHa 79) ===
Following the change of plan to retain the SaRo 45 cars, the target of conversion was shifted to third-class cars, and it was planned first to add doors to all the KuHa 47 cars and convert them to 85027–85036, following the KuHa 85 (85001–85026) produced by converting the 42-series KuHa 58 to commuter use. However, owing to intensified air raids and shortages of materials and labour, the plan was halted when two cars, 85030 and 85036, had been completed at the Oi Works before the war's end, creating gaps in the numbering. The window arrangement was dD13D4D31D1, and no window header was fitted above the added doors.

On April 22, 1949, the KuHa 85 was reclassified as KuHa 79 in order to hand over the designation “85” to the newly built 80 series cars. The old and new numbers correspond as follows.
79060 ← 85030 ← 47004
79066 ← 85036 ← 47010

=== Allied Forces cars ===
On the Yokosuka Line, second-class cars were still running at the war's end, but as the 32 series had only five SaRo 45 cars (45004, 45005, 45007, 45008, 45012), three SaHa 48 cars (48005–48007) became substitute second-class cars in December 1945.

In September 1946, all eight second-class cars, including the substitutes, were requisitioned by the Allied Forces; first, in November, the five SaRo 45 cars became “white-banded” cars as the “ALLIED FORCES SECTION,” their special compartments removed and simple partitions fitted at the car ends for use in Red Cross transport; the three substitute second-class SaHa 48 cars were also modified a month later along the lines of the SaRo 45, and in November 48008 was additionally requisitioned as an all-compartment Allied Forces car. These cars had their partitions removed in February 1947 to become “ALLIED FORCES CAR (AFC),” and at the end of that year a further ten SaHa 48 cars (48001, 48002, 48007, 48009, 48012, 48016, 48022, 48024, 48027, 48028) became AFCs. Thereafter, as of January 1, 1951, two SaRo 45 cars (45007, 45012) and eight SaHa 48 cars (48001, 48002, 48008, 48009, 48012, 48016, 48022, 48028) were Allied Forces cars, and ultimately the Allied Forces cars for the Yokosuka Line came to 18 cars of the 32 series (five SaRo 45 and 13 SaHa 48), plus eight cars of other series, for a cumulative total of 26.

The box seats of the SaHa 48 were too cramped for Allied servicemen, who were larger in build than Japanese, so the box seats were removed and replaced with longitudinal benches along the entire length, and the interior was painted light green and a greenish cream colour.

The Allied Forces cars were abolished before the San Francisco Peace Treaty came into effect on March 15, 1952.

=== Substitute second-class cars ===
Besides the three SaHa 48 cars (48005–48007) that became substitute second-class cars in 1945 as described above, when the coupling of second-class cars resumed on July 30, 1949, second-class cars were again in short supply, and substitute second-class cars were used, retaining the “SaHa” code but carrying a blue class band below the windows and a “2” class marking beside the passenger doors. In the 32 series, 14 SaHa 48 cars (48001–48003, 48005–48009, 48012, 48016, 48022, 48024, 48027, 48028) were made substitute second-class cars along with 11 cars of other series; of the SaHa 48 cars that had been converted to longitudinal benches while in AFC use, seven (48001, 48002, 48008, 48009, 48016, 48022, 48028) continued to be used with longitudinal benches.

=== Renewal repair and repainting ===
With the 80 series entering service in 1950, emergency servicing known as “renewal repair” was carried out on the Yokosuka Line cars to close the gap with the parallel 80 series. From fiscal 1949, work was carried out to strip the exterior paint and repaint the cars in “Yokosuka colour” (Suka colour), wash and re-varnish the wooden interior, restore and service the seats — restoring them to prewar standards — and change to pressed steel doors. The “Yokosuka colour” of the time had cream window surrounds (Cream No. 2) and blue cornice and side panels (Blue No. 2). The SaRo 45 cars, having remained second class and being in relatively good condition, did not receive renewal repair I, and only the paint colour was changed.

Before the renewal repair was carried out, a test paint scheme was applied to 32028: the front and right side had cream window surrounds and doors with wisteria-coloured cornice and side panels, the left side had orange window surrounds and doors with pale green cornice and side panels, and the gangway end was in the original grape colour No. 1 with yellow window surrounds on the left and grey on the right — it was dubbed the “ghost livery.”

=== Others ===
The low-voltage jumper electrical couplers on the cars allocated to the Tokyo Railway Bureau were fitted with three 7-core KE50s, but between fiscal 1946 and fiscal 1949 these were modified to two 12-core KE52s, the same as the cars allocated to the Osaka Railway Bureau. This made it possible to form mixed formations with the 42 series transferred in from the Osaka Railway Bureau from 1950 onward and the 70 series built from 1951 onward.

From fiscal 1952, Rochelle-salt telephone devices using the existing buzzer jumper wires were fitted for communication between crew members, and installation was completed on the Yokosuka Line cars within that fiscal year.
章节.Transfer away from the Yokosuka Line:
With the transfer of 42-series cars from the Keihanshin region to the Yokosuka Line in 1950 and the introduction of newly built 70-series cars from 1951, the surplus MoHa 32, KuHa 47, and SaHa 48 cars were transferred to the Minobu and Iida lines — electrified lines acquired during the war — within the jurisdiction of the Shizuoka Railway Bureau. On that occasion, in accordance with the bureau's policy, control motor cars were standardized to face down (even) and control trailers to face up (odd), and they were turned and modified by fitting cabs to the SaHa 48 cars. Meanwhile, the VIP car KuRo 49, its use declining after the war, was transferred to the Ito Line for general service, with the necessary modifications. The situation was as follows.

=== Fitting cabs to SaHa 48 (KuHa 47) ===
In transferring this series to the Iida Line, to make up for the shortage of lead cars, three SaHa 48 cars were turned in fiscal 1951 and had cabs fitted at the Toyokawa Branch Works. The old and new numbers correspond as follows, all facing up (odd). The cabs fitted were of the same 1,050 mm depth as the original KuHa 47, but the crew door position was shifted 70 mm rearward.
47011 ← 48005
47012 ← 48006
47013 ← 48007
Of these, 47011 made use of the donor car's windows and provided a window at the front centre while keeping the gangway dimensions, so the front window widths became irregular at 600 mm–800 mm–600 mm, but this was reworked during renewal repair II (described below) into the normal arrangement of equal-width windows. This car was completed as KuHa 48005 in October 1951 and used under that number for a little over three months.

In December 1959, it was decided to reorganize the cars converted from SaHa 48 under the numbers 47051 onward, so these cars, together with those converted later, were renumbered 47051, 47053, and 47055.

=== Incorporation of a rebuilt MoHa 30 (as KuHa 47) ===
MoHa 30173, which had been completely destroyed by fire in the Shimarō Tunnel between Uchibune and Yoseba on the Minobu Line on August 24, 1950, was rebuilt as a KuHa 47 at the Toyokawa Branch Works in 1952 and numbered 47023, following the cars converted from SaRoHa 66; under the December 1959 renumbering described above it was renumbered 47011 (second generation), following the newly built cars.

Nominally this car was a rebuild, but in effect it was a new build. Its basic layout followed the newly built KuHa 47 and the window arrangement was likewise dD1161D1, but the underframe was the UF134, the same as the KuHa 79 of the 72 series from the 300s onward and the SaRo 46 → SaRo 75 of the 70 series; the body was a newly built 20 m-class all-welded fully flat-ended body, and the roof height was 100 mm lower at 3,650 mm (with TR23 bogies). The seats followed the 80 series then being built, and a toilet was installed but of small dimensions, with the bowl set diagonally. The bogies were equalizer-type TR11s taken over from the SaHa 1 inherited from the Toyokawa Railway, but in 1966 they were exchanged with KuHa 16011, which had been transferred to the Iida Line, becoming TR23s. It received no renewal repair; only the roof ventilators were changed from Garland type to globe type in March 1959.

=== Fitting toilets to KuHa 47 ===
In 1951, when all eight KuHa 47 cars that had not undergone four-door conversion (47001–47003, 47005–47009) were transferred to the Minobu Line, toilets were fitted at the Toyokawa Branch Works, giving a capacity of 115 (80 seated). Compared with the cars converted from SaHa 48, the toilet was fitted on the opposite side, and the facing longitudinal bench was not converted to box seats — a further difference.

=== Conversion of KuRo 49 to general service (KuRoHa 49) ===
The VIP car KuRo 49, its use having declined after the war, was to be used for general service on the Ito Line, and in April 1953 it was converted to KuRoHa 49 at the Omiya Works. From the former special compartment through to the longitudinal bench beside the passenger door following the special compartment in the former attendants' room (second class) was made second class; the partition wall position was changed, the door in the old partition was removed, and the part including the remaining former attendants' room was made third class, giving a capacity of 73 (19 second-class and 54 third-class). In the third-class area the seat headrests were removed, and a door engine was fitted to the front door, which had previously had none.

On this occasion, since both cars faced down (even), 49001 was renumbered 49000 — in effect anticipating the revision of the type-designation regulations of June 1953 described below.
章节.Changes with the 1953 revision of the ve:
Under the revision of the vehicle type-designation regulations carried out on June 1, 1953, electric cars of 17 m-class overall length were assigned type numbers between 10 and 29, so in this series the MoHa 32 was combined with the MoHa 62 — likewise a two-door-per-side cross-seat car — to become the MoHa 14, and the 40 cars other than the five scrapped by that time were reclassified as MoHa 14. On this occasion only the type was changed and the numbers remained as they had been under MoHa 32, creating gaps in the numbering.

For the 20 m-class control cars and trailers, although types from other series were merged into this series, there was no change to the type numbers of the cars belonging to this series.
章节.Renewal Repair II and up to the 1959 ren:
=== Renewal Repair II and low-roof conversion of MoHa 14 ===
This series had its wartime and postwar wear-and-tear renovated and repaired from 1949, and a second renewal repair (Renewal Repair II), based on the lessons of the Sakuragicho accident of 1951, was carried out from 1954. The content of the renewal repair differed slightly by fiscal year, but the common items were as follows.
Replacement of ventilators from Garland type to globe type
Replacement of the interior woodwork
Fitting of the front run-number display window (three digits), excluding cars treated in 1954
Replacement of the pantograph with the PS13 (MoHa 14)
Change of gangway bellows from double to single and fitting of steel bellows seats
Conversion of the ceiling panels to light alloy
Change of interior lighting from one row to two rows

Renewal Repair II of the MoHa 14 was applied to Iida Line cars in 1954, to Minobu Line cars in 1955 and 1956, and again to Iida Line cars in 1957 and 1958. Among the Iida Line cars, those treated in 1954 kept the original straight front rain gutters and were not given run-indicator lights, while those treated in 1957 and 1958 had the front rain gutters changed to a curved form, a run-number display window fitted in the cornice on the assistant driver's side, and all front windows converted to H-rubber mounting. The Minobu Line renewed cars, in order to secure insulation clearance when passing through the tunnels with narrow construction clearances on that line, were given a low-roof structure with the roof lowered by 300 mm along the entire body length, greatly changing the impression of the end faces.

Through this modification the MoHa 14 was divided into two forms — the normal-roof cars for the Iida Line and the low-roof cars for the Minobu Line — but no distinction by number or the like was made at this point.

The status of Renewal Repair II on the MoHa 14 was as follows.
Fiscal 1954 (10 cars) – 14001, 14006, 14009, 14010, 14020, 14023, 14032, 14035, 14039, 14044 – for the Iida Line
Fiscal 1955 (11 cars) – 14002–14004, 14021, 14027, 14030, 14034, 14038, 14040, 14041, 14043 – for the Minobu Line
Fiscal 1956 (13 cars) – 14007, 14013–14017, 14019, 14024, 14025, 14028, 14036, 14037, 14042 – for the Minobu Line
Fiscal 1957 (3 cars) – 14018, 14029, 14031 – for the Iida Line
Fiscal 1958 (2 cars) – 14005, 14045 – for the Iida Line
Renewal Repair II on the KuHa 47 (excluding 47023) was carried out at the Toyokawa Branch Works in fiscal 1957 and fiscal 1958, when the front rain gutters were changed to a curved form.

The SaRo 45 underwent renewal repair at the Omiya Works from December 1953 to March of the following year, changing the roof ventilators from Garland to globe type; and from November 1956 to March of the following year it was modified by fitting a toilet and washroom at the rear end, with one side window on each side being filled in, giving a window arrangement of 2D2222222D1 and a capacity of 64. The seats were also replaced: the cross seats became 1,000 mm wide with armrests on both sides, and the longitudinal bench beside the door was enlarged from 1,900 mm to 1,950 mm in length.

=== Additional KuHa 47 converted from SaHa 48 ===
In fiscal 1953, six SaHa 48 cars had cabs fitted and were reclassified as KuHa 47. The donor cars were those that had been substitute second-class cars on the Yokosuka Line, and their interior seating was entirely longitudinal benches. All faced up (odd) and received odd numbers. Of the six, four — 47057, 47059, 47065, and 47067 — had their front rain gutters changed to a curved form during the conversion, but 47061 and 47063 retained the straight form until scrapping and attracted attention as oddities.

Subsequently, three more cars were converted in 1956, two in 1959, and two in 1961, making 16 cars converted to KuHa 47 in all. The five cars converted in 1956 and 1959 were for augmenting the Yokosuka Line's control cars, and the two converted in 1961 were for the Takasaki Railway Bureau, allocated to the Shin-Maebashi Electric Car Depot and used on the Takasaki Line as 80-series control cars, but ultimately all were used within the Shizuoka Railway Bureau's jurisdiction.

The cars converted in fiscal 1953 had cabs slightly deeper than those converted in fiscal 1951, at 1,050 mm, with a window provided at the rear of the cab, and a capacity of 130 (63 seated). The cars converted in 1959 and 1961 had front windows mounted in H-rubber; of these, on 47072–47074 the two on the driver's side were H-rubber mounted and the one on the assistant driver's side was an openable two-stage window.

The old and new numbers correspond as follows.

=== Conversion of KuRoHa 49 to intermediate trailer (SaRoHa 49) ===
The two former KuRo 49 cars that had been transferred to the Ito Line and used as KuRoHa 49 after half-compartment third-class conversion, since second-class cars came to be coupled in the middle of formations on that line, had their cabs removed and were converted to intermediate trailers when Renewal Repair II was carried out in 1956. The former third-class compartment (the former former attendants' room) was made a second-class compartment of capacity 32; on the former second-class side (the former former special compartment), the cab, toilet, and washroom were removed, the window arrangement changed to 322D2222D2, a gangway door fitted, and it became a third-class compartment of capacity 64 (44 seated). The passenger door positions were left unchanged, so the distinctive style was to some extent retained.

The type was changed to SaRoHa 49, and since the cab was removed and orientation no longer mattered, 49002 was renumbered 49001.

=== Conversion of SaHa 48 to a vehicle performance test car (KuYa 9020) ===
SaHa 48 no. 48008 had been burned out in an overhead-wire accident within Kurihama Station yard on June 26, 1951, while in Allied Forces use, and had been laid up long-term ever since. As the existing wooden test car KuYa 9010 no. 9010 was wearing out, this car was chosen as its replacement and was converted in April 1955 at the Oi Works into the electric-car performance test car KuYa 9020 for the Railway Technical Research Institute (now the Railway Technical Research Institute). The body had a low roof 3,495 mm high over its entire length and carried two pantographs; it became a double-ended car with a gangway door at the front, with a side window arrangement of d142181D'd (d121521D'd on the opposite side), and about half the interior length became a measuring room, along with a store, investigation room, workshop, overhead-wire observation room, darkroom, and wiring room; the bogies were TR43 with roller bearings. The body was initially painted dark green, later becoming grape colour with a yellow stripe, and the car's type number was also displayed in cut-out letters — the only such case on a JNR old-type electric car.

Under the 1959 renumbering described below it became KuYa 99 (KuYa 99000); afterwards one pantograph was removed and three distributed air-conditioning units were fitted, but with the completion of the successor MaYa 11 in 1966, it was scrapped in 1976.
章节.Changes with the June 1959 revision of t:
Effective June 1, 1959, a revision of the vehicle type-designation regulations was carried out to move the type designations of the new-performance (second-generation) electric cars to a separate system. In this revision, control motor cars with a cab and intermediate motor cars without a cab were separated; the prefix “Kumo” was newly established for control motor cars, and types previously indicated by number alone were changed to be designated together with the conventional prefix. In addition, department (service) cars, which had previously been incorporated into the miscellaneous-type numbering system, were brought into the standard-type numbering system.

As a result, of the former 32 series, the MoHa 14 became KuMoHa 14, and the department car KuYa 9020 (formerly 48008) became KuYa 99.
章节.Changes from the December 1959 renumberi:
Renewal Repair II had divided the KuMoHa 14 into normal-roof cars and low-roof cars for the Minobu Line, but since no distinction was made by number, the two types were mixed at the Fuji Electric Car Depot, which handled cars for both the Minobu Line and Tokaido Line local trains, causing inconvenience in operation. Accordingly, by Works Instruction No. 1528 dated December 22, 1959, the low-roof cars were assigned to the 800 series and the normal-roof cars were also renumbered in a reorganization. At the same time, the KuMoHaYuni 44 and the KuHa 47 converted from trailers were also renumbered. The old and new numbers of the KuMoHa 14 and KuHa 47 belonging to this series correspond as follows.

章节.Developments from 1960 onward:
=== Change from three-class to two-class system ===
From July 1, 1960, the class system changed from three classes — first, second, and third — to a two-class system comprising first class (the former second and first classes merged) and second class (converted from the former third class). There was no change of type in this series, but the usage prefix “Ro” came to denote first-class cars and “Ha” second-class cars.

=== Conversion of SaRoHa 49 to second-class car (SaHa 48) ===
The SaRoHa 49 converted to a trailer continued in use on the Ito Line, but as first-class usage increased it was replaced by the SaRo 15 in October 1962 and used as a substitute second-class car with its interior equipment unchanged. In March–April of the following year, 1963, it was converted at the Omiya Works into an all-compartment second-class car and incorporated into the SaHa 48, assigned to the 40 series; the passenger door at the body centre was moved to the car end, giving a window arrangement of 2D1222222D2, a capacity of 124 (82 seated), and fluorescent interior lighting. Both cars were transferred to the Okayama Railway Bureau in 1966 and used on the Uno Line with 51-series and SaHa 58 cars.

The old and new numbers correspond as follows.
SaHa 48040 ← SaRoHa 49000
SaHa 48041 ← SaRoHa 49001

=== Conversion of KuHa 47 to three-door (KuHa 68) ===
The two KuHa 47 cars remaining on the Yokosuka Line were, between 1963 and 1964, converted to three-door cars by adding a passenger door at the body centre — along with the KuMoHa 43, KuMoHa 53, and SaHa 48 (ex-52 series) — to cope with intensified commuter traffic; KuHa 47002, then in use on the Iida Line, received the same modification at the same time, giving a window arrangement of dD16D161D1 for both, and capacities — differing because of the seat layout opposite the toilet — of 116 (68 seated) for the former and 116 (67 seated) for the latter, with fluorescent interior lighting. The cars modified under this work were incorporated into the KuHa 68, a three-door cross-seat control car; cars converted from the original KuHa 47 were assigned to the 200 series, and those converted from the SaHa 48 into lead cars to the 210 series.

The old and new numbers correspond as follows.
KuHa 68200 ← KuHa 47002
KuHa 68210 ← KuHa 47072
KuHa 68211 ← KuHa 47073
Thereafter, with the introduction of the 113 series onto the Yokosuka Line, they were transferred to the Niigata area along with the 70 series, and Iida Line 68200 (← 47002) was also transferred to the Niigata area at the same time.

=== Conversion of SaRo 45 to second-class car (SaHa 45) ===
The SaRo 45 was the last of this series to remain in use on the Yokosuka Line, but when it was decided to downgrade the old-type first-class cars equivalent to the “Namiro” category, all five cars (45004, 45005, 45007, 45008, 45012) were renamed as the second-class SaHa 45 in August 1964 and March 1965 (numbers unchanged). No change was made to the interior equipment, which remained as in first-class days, giving a capacity of 102 (64 seated). This type was transferred, simultaneously with the downgrading, to the Minobu and Iida lines of the Shizuoka Railway Bureau, but it soon left the Iida Line, some cars later moving to the Oito Line, where they were used until 1981 — the very end of the so-called old-type JNR electric cars.

=== Fitting toilets to SaHa 78 ===
With the electrification of the Gotemba Line in April 1968, toilets were installed at the Hamamatsu Works on the SaHa 78 cars used on that line. Among the four-door cars converted from this series, two (one ex-SaRo 45 and one ex-SaRoHa 46) were modified, giving a capacity of 145 (51 seated), and they were renumbered into the 400 series by a notice dated November 14, 1968. The old and new numbers correspond as follows.
SaHa 78400 ← SaHa 78018
SaHa 78401 ← SaHa 78023
章节.Operation:
=== Yokosuka Line ===
On the Yokosuka Line, the timetable revised on April 1, 1925, when steam locomotives hauled the trains, showed 110 minutes between Tokyo and Yokosuka; the timetable revised on September 15, 1929, under electric-locomotive haulage, showed 85 minutes; and the timetable revised on March 15, 1930, with electric multiple-unit operation, listed 42 up and 41 down trains (one round trip between Tokyo and Ofuna) at 68 minutes between Tokyo and Yokosuka. In the timetable revised on October 1, 1931, after the introduction of the 32 series, trains ran between Tokyo and Yokosuka in 68 minutes, with 44 on weekdays and 36 on holidays, at 15-minute intervals in the morning and evening on weekdays and 30-minute intervals at other times; the stopping stations were Tokyo, Shimbashi, Shinagawa, Yokohama, Hodogaya, Totsuka, Ofuna, Kita-Kamakura, Kamakura, Zushi, Taura, and Yokosuka.

At the start of operation the basic formation was 4–5 cars and the supplementary formation 2–3 cars; the formations around April 1932 were as follows. The maximum formation length for electric trains at that time was seven cars on the Chuo Line (Tokyo–Tachikawa), eight on the Yamanote Line (Tokyo–Tabata–Akabane) and Keihin Line (Tokyo–Tsurumi), and seven on the Yokosuka Line (Tokyo–Yokosuka); the schedule speed of electric trains in 1935 was fastest on the Yokosuka Line at 55.1 km/h, followed by 52.0 km/h between Suita and Akashi on the Tokaido Line and 48.0 km/h between Kobe and Akashi on the Sanyo Line.

7 basic formations (4 diagrams), 2 supplementary formations (2 diagrams)

Thereafter, in conjunction with the introduction of the MoHaYuni 44 in 1935 and the fitting of toilets to the SaRoHa 46 and SaHa 48, from that year or 1937 the basic formation was standardized at four cars and the supplementary formation at three cars, as follows; as replacements for the shortfall in SaRo 45 cars, SaRo 37 cars 37001 and 37002 of the 31 series were transferred to the Yokosuka Line.
Basic formation

Later, to increase capacity, some basic formations were lengthened to five cars, and formations such as the following were also operated.
With baggage/mail cars

During this period, from April 1942 a shuttle service was operated between Zushi and Yokosuka, with trains running at 7–10 minute intervals on that section. On April 1, 1944, the section between Yokosuka and Kurihama opened, and the down-direction timetable revised on October 11 of that year listed 51 trains, rising to 60 when shuttle trains were included. In this timetable there were 23 trains between Tokyo and Kurihama, 22 between Tokyo and Yokosuka, 3 between Yokohama and Yokosuka, and one each between Shinagawa and Yokosuka, Ofuna and Yokosuka, and Ofuna and Kurihama, of which 15 carried second-class cars.

The Ministry of Railways' second-class cars were abolished on October 31, 1938, except on the Kansai express services and the Yokosuka Line; accordingly, KuRoHa 69 cars 69001 and 69002 of the 51 series were transferred to the Yokosuka Line. The Yokosuka Line's second-class cars were then abolished once on April 1, 1944, when the Yokosuka–Kurihama section opened, but owing to the special circumstance of the naval port at Yokosuka, the coupling of second-class cars resumed on August 16 at the Navy's request. As noted above, because conversion to commuter cars was proceeding for all the SaRoHa 46 and some of the SaRo 45, the coupling of second-class cars was limited to some trains, and besides the SaRo 45, two SaRo 37 and one KuRoHa 69 were used.

After the war, on September 23, 1946, all second-class cars became Allied Forces cars, and from November 2 they became white-banded cars for the exclusive use of the Allied Forces. At first they were the “U. S. Army Section,” later becoming the “Allied Forces Section (AFS)” or “Allied Forces Car (AFC)”; in August 1947 Japanese passengers were permitted to ride when seats were vacant, on July 30, 1949 the coupling of second-class cars resumed, and in September they were coupled to all formations, with one AFC and one second-class car included in each formation, after which the white-banded cars were abolished in March 1952. As of June 1, 1947, trains ran in seven-car formations with one AFC, as follows.
9 formations in service, 1 spare, 2 under inspection

Before the war the Yokosuka Line was operated mainly with the 32 series, but in the final stage of the war the Tamachi Electric Car Depot, which had jurisdiction over the line, evacuated cars in good condition to other lines and instead transferred poorly conditioned cars to the Yokosuka Line; from June 1945 the 32 series was evacuated to the Joban, Akabane, and Yokohama lines, and by September 1947 they had returned to the Tamachi Depot. Amid these developments, the 40 series arrived during the war and, in the postwar confusion, the 30 and 50 series as well; from 1949 the 63 series arrived, and from 1950 the 42 and 52 series that had been used in Kansai, and they were operated together with the 32 series. Thereafter, as the first ten 70-series cars were introduced in March 1951 and further cars were added, the MoHa 32 was progressively transferred to the Iida and Minobu lines from March 1951, while some of the SaRo 45 and SaHa 48 formed formations with these types and continued in service on the Yokosuka Line. The allocation of the Tamachi Electric Car Depot (excluding the Ito sub-depot), which had jurisdiction over the Yokosuka Line (and Tokaido Line) electric cars in the postwar 1940s and 1950s, was as follows.

During this period, in June 1947 the maximum formation became nine cars (a seven-car basic formation plus a two-car supplementary formation), and from February 1949 trains ran in formations of up to ten cars (seven basic plus three supplementary). After the introduction of the 70 series in March 1951, trains ran in 11–12 car formations combining a seven-car basic formation with a four- or five-car supplementary formation, and the coupling and uncoupling work for the supplementary formation at Zushi Station was carried out from December 17. Thereafter, on February 1, 1959, the basic formation was changed to six cars, and trains ran in 12-car formations combining these, while two-car operation between Yokosuka and Kurihama was also begun.

On the Yokosuka Line, the KuHa 47, SaRo 45, and SaHa 48 were ultimately used until they were replaced by the 113 series in the mid-1960s; KuHa 68210 and 68211 (three-door conversions of KuHa 47072 and 47073) and SaHa 48018 and 48027 remained on the Yokosuka Line until 1964, and SaRo 45004, 45005, 45007, 45008, and 45012 until 1964–1965.

=== Outside the Yokosuka Line (up to around 1950) ===
Around 1935, before the war, they were used on spring and autumn special trains on the Chuo Line, and also on trains running through to Mitake Station on the Ome Electric Railway. In addition, with the electrification of the Yokohama Line in October 1942, three to five MoHa 32 cars were lent to the Higashi-Kanagawa Electric Car Depot.

During and after the war, some cars ran on the Yokohama, Joban, and Akabane lines as a result of the aforementioned redeployment, and at Higashi-Kanagawa and Shinagawa, MoHa 32 cars were loaded with recovery equipment and used as substitute rescue cars.

From November 1948, after the war, operation by Yokosuka Line cars began as far as Hiratsuka on the Tokaido Line; and when the Takasaki Line was electrified on April 1, 1952, with electric operation as far as Kumagaya, a four-car Yokosuka Line formation was lent out. On the Ito Line, where electric operation began on May 15, 1949, four MoHa 32 and three KuHa 47 of the 32 series were allocated to the Ito sub-depot of the Tamachi Electric Car Depot for shuttle services, along with two MoHaYuni 44 of the 42 series; thereafter, as of July 1, 1953, two KuRoHa 49 were still allocated and operated together with seven 42-series and two 40-series cars.

=== KuRo 49 ===
The KuRo 49 Imperial-family VIP car operated in two-car formations with a MoHa 32, coupled at the Tokyo end of revenue trains, and the coupler of the MoHa 32 — which formed the head of the formation — was painted silver. This type was basically for imperial passenger trains but was also used for special imperial trains; on March 25, 1941, the electric train carrying Emperor Showa between Tokyo and Yokosuka was the first imperial train operated by electric multiple unit, using 49001 and other 32-series cars. The formation that day was as follows, and the car continued to be used for imperial trains thereafter.

This type was also operated outside the Yokosuka Line, including in the Kansai region — for example between Higashi-Kishiwada and Higashi-Wakayama on the Hanwa Line on June 7, 1947, and between Yotsuya and Yose Station (now Sagamiko Station) on July 17 of the same year. The formation on June 7 was as follows, with the top row being the pilot car, the middle row the main formation, and the bottom row the spare formation.
章节.Scrapping:
Of the 32 series, the cars that did not undergo door-addition conversion were concentrated within the Shizuoka Railway Bureau's jurisdiction, except for some SaHa 48 used at Okayama and some SaHa 45 used on the Oito Line, and were used interchangeably with the 40, 51, and 52 series. Full-scale replacement of the aging fleet began in 1967, starting with the 17 m-class, low-capacity KuMoHa 14, which was replaced by KuMoHa 51 and KuMoHa 60 cars transferred in from the Kansai region. The 20 m-class control cars and trailers continued in use but were scrapped by 1983 as they were replaced by new-performance electric cars.

The replacement timings were: the Uno Line in 1976, the Oito and Minobu lines in 1981, and the Iida Line in 1978 and 1983.

章节.Transfer:
Because the 32 series was used by JNR for a relatively long period, apart from the sale of war-damaged and accident cars immediately after the end of the Pacific War, only two KuMoHa 14 cars (14007, 14009) were transferred to Fuji Kyuko.

=== Fuji Kyuko 7000 series ===
The two KuMoHa 14 cars (14007, 14009) transferred in 1969, after receiving updates such as aluminium-sash window frames, became MoHa 7031 and MoHa 7032 of the 7000 series, and formed formations with KuHa 7061 and 7062 — former KuHa 16 cars (of the old 50-series group, 16425 and 16467, respectively ex-65033 and 65089) transferred at the same time — and were used on the Fuji Kyuko Line together with MoHa 7033 and KuHa 7063, former KuMoHa 12 and KuHa 16 cars transferred in 1971. Subsequently, with the introduction of the 5700 series (ex-Odakyu 2200, 2220, 2300, and 2320 series), they were scrapped in 1983.
